brief.head: Built for episode 100
brief.text: Amit Varma told a friend starting a podcast to think not of what listeners find in episode one but what they can binge by episode hundred. {114-S01}

brief.head: Hello, the poor
brief.text: Every human welfare indicator tracks per capita GDP far more than redistribution, Amit Varma noted. So when economists talk GDP, he said, they are talking about the poor. {114-C03}

brief.head: Twelve branches a year
brief.text: All foreign banks in India together could open twelve branches a year, Ajay Shah said, raised to eighteen in a supposed act of great liberalisation. {114-S03}

brief.head: Pour the concrete
brief.text: A tariff cut can always be reversed, Ajay Shah said. What steadies firms is a credible team that explains its logic and admits problems honestly. {114-C15}

brief.head: Whispers won’t do
brief.text: Whispering to a joint secretary changes little, Ajay Shah argued. Policy shifts when new ideas change the climate of opinion upstream, as before 1991. {114-C18}

thought.who: Ajay Shah, to every enthusiastic nationalist demanding an Indian CPU or LLM

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India after the tariffs
lead.head: Mind the other two-thirds
body: Donald Trump’s tariffs on India came in two instalments: 25 per cent on everything but electronics and pharma, then another 25 per cent, supposedly to punish India for buying Russian crude. Fifty per cent, Ajay Shah said, is “a lot and it’s a mess”.
So Shah and Amit Varma took up the question their audience kept asking: what should India do? Varma promised an episode that was timely, but also a “first draft of history” of a pivotal moment.

Shah’s answer, built on an essay he wrote with Vijay Kelkar, was a roadmap in three parts: deep trade agreements with the rest of the rich world, reform at home, and hard-headed dealings with America and China.
## The best twenty years
The starting point was 1991 to 2011, when India’s GDP grew about fourfold. “That is simply the biggest shining success in 5,000 years of Indian history,” Shah said. {114-C01}
It came from abroad: technology, knowledge, capital and markets, once the Indian state got out of the way.
Yet India never played in good faith, Shah said. Its officials spoiled trade talks and its rules were unfair to foreign firms. The West indulged it, assuming India would grow up.
Right-wing populism has ended that patience. “What we see with Trump today is to some extent made in India,” he said. {114-C04}
## Beyond America

America, Shah pointed out, is only about a third of the trade of the advanced economies. The rest, from Western Europe and Canada to Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Australia, is rich, democratic and still open.
Democracies keep treaties for five, ten or twenty years, the horizon firms need to invest. “The problem in working with authoritarian countries is that strongmen are untrustworthy,” he said.

So India should help found a new globalisation, built on deep trade agreements that bind members to fair play on regulation, intellectual property, capital and foreign firms. {114-C09} That means an end to third-worldism and to “500 red lines”.
At home the list is long: a clean GST and carbon tax, reformed regulators, working courts and cities, an agriculture that is no longer a holy cow, and finance that can fund big projects.

Shah also wants resilience, not autarky: fiscal prudence, an RBI devoted only to inflation targeting, and a rupee that genuinely floats. “A floating exchange rate is a shock absorber,” he said. {114-C14}
## Pride, pessimism and speed
With Trump and with Xi Jinping alike, Shah argued, India must negotiate from expertise rather than pride. If flattery works on Trump, India should flatter.

Varma agreed, but confessed to pessimism. Politicians, he feared, would answer a 50 per cent tariff with a 60 per cent one and prefer narrative battles to hard global work, while the opposition opposes for the sake of opposing.
His remedy is for people who agree to be vocal, as outsiders had to be in the 1990s when the reformers inside government could not sell reform themselves.
Shah ended with a playbook for firms: treat America like an emerging market, chase the rest of the rich world, and move fast. “The race will go to the nimble,” he said. {114-C19}
Varma found hope in that. Indian firms, he said, have long found their way around bad policy. “We can adjust, we can be nimble.”

second.label: The Red Sea
second.head: Not a tanker in sight
second.deck: A map of LNG tankers showed Ajay Shah how India’s route to Europe closed
body: Ajay Shah’s friend Ashima Sharma showed him a map of the world with each of its roughly 700 LNG tankers plotted as a dot. Not one was in the Red Sea. {114-S04}

The Houthis are choking the route, Shah said, and some ships pay them ransom to pass. {#ransom} Since 1945 the US Navy has run freedom of navigation operations around the world. This time, he said, it has stepped back.

For India that is a heavy blow. Its natural market for goods is Europe, and the Suez Canal, which he dated to 1869, is “the magic”: the short way there, instead of the long route round the Cape of Good Hope. {114-J14}

quote.text: And there was not a single tanker in the Red Sea. There is just such a mind blowing moment for me.

third.head: A panipuri theory of risk
body: At a conference that Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik organised at NIPFP, a Chilean economist explained capital account convertibility with two characters. {114-S05}

One is an 85-year-old who never leaves the house or eats out, for fear of falling sick. The other is a 12-year-old who flies out of the door, tumbles on the ground, plays with frogs and eats panipuri on the roadside. The child falls sick all the time, and bounces back. {#bounce}
Shah wants India to be the child. The reflexive urge to hide behind a high fence, he said, comes from insecurity. Resilience means taking shocks and bouncing back.
India, he pointed out, has already rolled with the 1991 crisis, the nuclear tests, Y2K, the Asian crisis and 2008. {#overcame} “India is not inferior,” he said.
third.caption: the 85-year-old and the 12-year-old

p2.title: What India should do
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s roadmap for India after the tariffs, argued out with Amit Varma chapter by chapter

sections.label: The good times
sections.head: Twenty years, four gifts
sections.caption: India’s best twenty years, 1991 to 2011
body: Between 1991 and 2011, Ajay Shah said, India’s GDP grew about fourfold. To find a better twenty years, you would have to go back to Mohenjo-daro. {114-C01}
The gains came from the West once the Indian state took down its own barriers. By the West he means liberal democracies, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan included.

First came technology: machine tools, CPUs, operating systems, fibre and the internet. Nobody demanded an Indian CPU or a subsidised chip fab then, and Shah sees no need for an Indian LLM now. If Indians can help build a CPU, great; if not, buy other people’s. {114-C02}
## Knowledge walks out the gate

Next came knowledge, from Indians who studied and, above all, worked abroad, and from foreign firms in India. Shah has “no shame in saying that Hyundai knew more about how to make cars than Tata Motors”. Those who learned at Hyundai’s factory went on to Tata Motors, ancillary firms and EV projects. {114-S02}
Then finance. Foreign capital backed the new economy before Indian investors woke up to it. “It was the foreigners that made Infosys great,” he said. And finally, markets abroad.
~ Amit Varma drew the moral. Poverty is humanity’s default state, and growth in those years lifted hundreds of millions out of it, so getting policy right is “a moral imperative”.

quote.text: And that is simply the biggest shining success in 5,000 years of Indian history.

sections.label: India and America
sections.head: Newton’s law of trade
sections.caption: the gravity model of trade
body: Trade, Ajay Shah said, behaves like Newton’s gravitation: it rises with the product of two countries’ GDPs and falls with the square of the distance between them. {114-C05}
That is bad news for goods bound for America. The United States is vast but fairly inward-looking, and it is the farthest place India can ship to. From China or Japan, Los Angeles is a short hop.
Amit Varma drew his own conclusion: the closer he and Shah get to each other, the more likely they are to hug. {114-J01}
## Weightless photons

Services escape gravity. On fibre-optic cables photons fly, Shah said, correcting himself after a YouTube commenter accused him of always saying electrons. Photons are weightless, so California is not far. {114-J09}

Hence services exports to America thrive while goods struggle. Of about $460 billion in Indian goods exports, around $85 billion go to the US, and about $65 billion face the 50 per cent tariff. {#exports}
~ That is about 15 per cent of goods exports, Shah said. The dynamic action is in services, which bring in about $370 billion.

quote.text: the trade between two countries is proportional to the product of their two GDPs divided by the distance between them squared.

sections.label: The American wound
sections.head: A sound US is India’s business
sections.caption: why India needs a healthy America
body: Amit Varma is an anti-tariff absolutist. Tariffs, he said, are always bad for your own people, which is why India should have none at all.
Ajay Shah agreed that America is hurting itself, though a once-in-a-century AI capex boom hides it. Split the Magnificent 7 from the rest of the S&P 500, he said, and the pain shows.

He listed the harms: rising prices and unanchored inflation; uncertainty that chokes investment and makes America “an emerging market”; cost shocks for exporters reliant on imported inputs; and a fraying safe-haven dollar.

That matters to India more than the tariff, he argued. India needs American finance, services demand, technology, the GCCs built by American firms, and a US Navy that keeps the Red Sea open. {114-C06}
## Not a switch
Nor will the tariff switch off $65 billion of exports at a stroke, Shah said. {114-C07}

A $10 shirt hit by a 50 per cent tariff looks like game over. {#shirt} But Vietnam takes the American order and India picks up the German buyer Vietnam used to serve. The rupee falls, firms absorb some margin, and workers move to other employers.
~ Varma added Henry Hazlitt’s broken window: the adjustments do not make the tariff harmless, because what is unseen is what would have happened without it. {114-R10}

quote.text: The world needs a sound United States. India needs a sound United States.

sections.label: A new globalisation
sections.head: Founders of a new club
sections.caption: deep trade agreements
body: America is only about a third of advanced-economy trade, Ajay Shah said. India should embrace the rest: Western Europe, Canada, Chile, Australia, New Zealand, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea and Israel.

They are rich, and they are democracies, so a treaty signed with them holds for five, ten or twenty years. Strongmen rule by discretion and change their minds overnight, and firms simply wait and watch. {114-C08}

The WTO failed, he said, because countries could cheat. A deep trade agreement binds members to fair play on regulation, intellectual property, capital and foreign firms. The EU is one; the TPP, which eleven countries pursued after Trump walked out, is another.
## No more third-worldism

India, Shah argued, should help found a new coalition of ten or twenty like-minded countries, and start upgrading its trade agreement with the UK into a deep one now, since talks take two or three years. {114-C09}

That means dropping anti-colonial rhetoric and the habit of torpedoing negotiations. Unfairness to foreigners at home, he warned, feeds hostile populists abroad, who already have a 20 per cent vote share in Germany. {#germany}

~ The prize could be concrete: German carmakers building components and software in India, Japanese electronics firms pairing with Indian factories, Korean shipyards, and frugal defence partners in Ukraine, Poland and South Korea. {114-C11}

quote.text: India can and should be a founder member of a new globalization.

sections.label: Reform at home
sections.head: Trade policy starts at home
sections.caption: domestic reform as trade policy
body: The second pillar of Ajay Shah’s plan is domestic, and each item, he said, ties back to winning the 66 per cent.

First, taxes. Non-residents are not India’s tax base, so exporters should get back every indirect tax paid along the chain. India’s GST has “birth defects”, he said, and the world is converging on a clean GST plus an auditable carbon tax that meet at the border. {114-C12}

Then regulators, who have become a new central planning system; courts, so that penalties from foreign buyers can be passed on to Indian vendors; and cities. A factory of 20,000 workers on three shifts, he said, needs 60,000 households nearby. {#shifts}
Agriculture cannot stay a holy cow. “Once we adopt red lines, you basically stop doing diplomacy,” Shah said. {114-C10}
## Trust as currency
He wants resilience, not autarky: fiscal prudence, an RBI devoted only to inflation targeting, a floating rupee and banks that don’t blow up.

Policy, he added, is an incomplete contract. A tariff cut can be reversed, so credibility comes from a visible team that explains its logic honestly, not a fatwa handed down like the Ten Commandments. {114-J18}
~ Foreign firms also need fair treatment, through OECD-style tax treaties and bilateral investment treaties.

quote.text: The price of goods on a ship on the high seas should be minus Indian taxation.

sections.label: America and China
sections.head: Flatter, if flattery works
sections.caption: dealing with Trump and Xi Jinping
body: India cannot do autarky with the United States or with China, Ajay Shah said. It has to negotiate, and “there is no place for pride”.
With Trump, that means deep expertise on MAGA and the new American right. If flattery will get India past him, Shah said, India should flatter. {114-R22}
With China, slogans of friendship won’t do after Doklam and Galwan and Chinese overproduction. India needs a brains trust that can get inside Xi Jinping’s mind and work out the carrots and sticks.
Twitter one-liners, autarky and “strategic autonomy”, he said, serve moral purity, not the national interest.
## Varma’s three worries
Amit Varma agreed, and is pessimistic all the same. Trade is never zero-sum, he said, yet the reflex to answer a 50 per cent tariff with 60 per cent turns it into a game both sides lose. {114-C17}

Leaders, he feared, would prefer narrative battles, like the TikTok ban, to hard global work, and an opposition that opposes everything leaves no room for the cross-party statesmanship of 1991 to 2011.
~ Shah’s answer was a theory of change: work upstream of the policymaker, on ideas and the climate of opinion. Varma cited Andrew Breitbart: politics is downstream of culture. {114-J19}

quote.text: It is not a question of pride. It is a question of Indian self-interest.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah and Vijay Kelkar wrote *Indian economic strategy in the new globalisation* for the LEAP blog, pulling together columns by Sajjid Z Chinoy, TN Ninan, Rajeswari Sengupta, Mihir S Sharma and others into one coherent argument. {114-R02}

contQuote.text: Each of these points is directly connected to the project of Indian deep globalization so that we can do more with the sixty six so as to make up for the problems of the thirty three.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Vicks, Soviet factories, a stealthy reform and an argument over lunch

stories.start: In my episode with Gurchirandas he told me this wonderful story
stories.end: every employee of the company made a down payment on a house
stories.caption: the Vicks VapoRub story
stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a crisis at Richardson Vicks
stories.head: The rub that dodged a tax
body: Gurcharan Das was running Richardson Vicks in India, around the early 1980s by Amit Varma’s reckoning, when the government slapped a new levy on certain medicines. One of them was Vicks VapoRub, and the tax would make it unprofitable overnight.
Das called his top people to a crisis meeting. Then someone in a corner quietly pointed out two things. VapoRub’s formulation was compatible with Ayurveda. And Ayurveda was not taxed.

Within 24 hours the company filed a proposal for an entirely new medicine, which was entirely the same medicine, now called an Ayurvedic rub. {#vicks24} The bureaucrat saw what they were up to, Varma said, but it was within the letter of the law, and it passed.
Das saw something bigger. As an Ayurvedic product, VapoRub could be sold at about four million outlets, paanwalas included, instead of about 50,000 medical shops. {#outlets}

So he gave stock options to every single person in the company, down to the lowest peon. {#options} The company registrar, who had never heard of stock options, suspected a scam. Some staff could not afford Rs 20 a share, so the company lent them the money.
If he remembered correctly, Varma said, the share price rose forty times within a year, and every employee made a down payment on a house. {114-S09}
~ What did it tell him? “Indians do jugaad well,” Varma concluded, though he does not usually celebrate it.
stories.why: Indian firms can be remarkably nimble under bad policy. Firms should not have to resort to jugaad, Varma said, but the story gives him hope that Indian business can adapt to the tariff shock.

stories.start: Okay, you know that uh on the 21st of June 1941
stories.end: dismantle an entire factory and put it into a zero tariff country
stories.caption: the Soviet factories that moved
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s lesson for tariff-hit firms, from 1941
stories.head: Have factory, will travel
body: On 21 June 1941, Ajay Shah recounted, the German army invaded the USSR and pushed about a thousand kilometres into Soviet territory, through the country’s industrial heartland.
Under fire, the Soviets dismantled entire factories, carried them away to Central Asia, reassembled them and restarted war production. {114-S08}

“That’s how I feel today,” Shah said. If there is a 50 per cent tariff on India, dismantle the factory and take it to Sri Lanka. How difficult is it, he asked, to put a whole factory into a zero-tariff country?
~ His point was about speed. In a fluctuating world, Indian firms that move faster than global rivals could find that nimbleness is “a killer app”. {114-C19}
stories.why: In a world like this, a factory’s address is a choice, not a law of nature. Tariffs could swing to 300, Shah warned, and a Senate bill proposes secondary oil tariffs of 500 per cent. {#senate}

stories.start: I did a great episode of the Seen and the Unseen recently with Gurchirandas
stories.end: I want you to say it outside. So it needed to be sold
stories.caption: reforms by stealth
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on why the 1991 reforms needed salesmen
stories.head: Manmohan’s outsourced sales pitch
body: In the early 1990s, Amit Varma said, Gurcharan Das wrote to Manmohan Singh with a question: why are you doing reforms by stealth?

Narasimha Rao and Manmohan Singh sold the reforms as a better form of socialism that Nehru and Indira would have liked. They were really a repudiation of socialism, but the reformers were scared of going against the party line and its heroes. Deng Xiaoping and Margaret Thatcher, Das pointed out, sold their reforms openly. {114-J21}
Manmohan Singh’s reply was short. “You come back and sell them for me.” {114-S07}

~ Naushad Forbes told Varma a similar story. After a meeting of industrialists with Manmohan Singh, then finance minister, Manmohan took Forbes aside: everything he had said in the meeting, he wanted said outside. {#forbes}
stories.why: Reform needs public salesmanship, and insiders often cannot do it. That, Varma argued, makes it the job of citizens and outside voices: if you agree with these ideas, you cannot be a passive observer.
stories.postscript: Varma’s episode with Montek Singh Ahluwalia, he said, traces how reformers built these ideas from the late 1970s.

stories.start: an argument I had with our good friend the brilliant Natin Pae
stories.end: remains a friend. We survived that uh grievous uh incident
stories.caption: the argument with Nitin Pai
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a lunch, a tariff and a Nobel nomination
stories.head: A bow too far for Nitin Pai
body: Just after the first 25 per cent tariff, Amit Varma had lunch with Nitin Pai, Narendra Shenoy and Sudhir Sarnobat.

The inside dope, Varma said, was that Trump would not have imposed the tariff if Modi had simply agreed that Trump helped the peace process between India and Pakistan. Pakistan had played along and nominated Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize.
Varma argued Modi should kowtow if he had to. “It’s not a matter of ego or pride,” he said. “You just do what’s good for the country.” The tariff, he said, hurt both Indians and Americans. {114-S06}
~ Pai was completely against it, and the episode cut to a video of his reaction. But he “remains a friend”, Varma said. “We survived that grievous incident.” {114-J06}
stories.why: For Varma, the test of a leader is national welfare, not national ego. Pride is a cost citizens pay, which is also Ajay Shah’s case for choosing prosperity over pride. {114-R22}
